newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banker faces trial on money laundering charge.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banker faces trial on money laundering charge.

text.p: A Zurich court hearing one of Switzerland's biggest money laundering cases is set to hand down a ruling that will test government efforts to lift the veil of secrecy around the country's banking system.

The Swiss prosecutor confirmed that banker Josef Oberholzer went on trial this week accused of managing Swiss accounts for Colombian drug smugglers starting in the 1970s. The portfolio he oversaw had grown to $150 million by the time he was arrested and the money was seized in 1994.
Oberholzer, a former Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) vice-director, is the highest-ranking banker in Switzerland to have been charged to date with such a crime.
The $150 million was the largest haul of alleged laundered money ever in Switzerland. The case is the first big test of new laws to combat money laundering that Switzerland passed in 1990.
The case is also a model for prosecutors because the money flowed from Colombia to New York, then to Panama and finally to Switzerland, Zurich district attorney Dieter Jann said on Wednesday.
"This case is very important. It's the first case in Switzerland following the classic model," Jann told Reuters.
"It is decisive because of the changes in the law and we are very eager to hear the outcome," he added.

Oberholzer was not available for comment, but Swiss media quoted him as testifying that he never asked where the money in question came from. "I was happy that new money was coming in again," the Blick daily quoted him as saying.
Oberholzer's attorney, Christoph Hohler, has contended his client was only doing what other Swiss bankers did at the time.
The Swiss have been trying to shake their reputation as bankers to the world's dictators and drug runners since the start of this decade.

During the 1970s and 1980s, Switzerland's combination of political stability and banking discretion made it the financial centre of choice for customers including the late Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos to Panamanian dictator Manuel Noriega.
Pressure by the United States on a number of countries, including Switzerland, to crack down on the proceeds of crime encouraged Berne to outlaw money laundering in 1990.

In 1994 Switzerland passed another law giving bankers the right to breach the country's legendary banking secrecy laws and report suspicious transactions to authorities. Even tougher measures are still working their way through parliament.
But while the tougher laws ensure banks reject suitcases full of drug money, they do not address funds accepted years ago when controls were less thorough or did not exist at all.

If convicted, Oberholzer faces a two-and-a-half year prison sentence and a fine of 200,000 Swiss francs ($135,000). Prosecutors are also seeking the return of some 1.3 million francs he allegedly got in commissions for managing the drug cartel's funds.
A ruling is expected within two weeks, Jann said.
UBS is not involved as a party in the trial.

Alleged drug smuggler Julio Cesar Nasser is still at large. His former wife, Sheila Miriam Arana Nasser, is serving a 12-year sentence in Florida after pleading guilty in 1995 to U.S. federal conspiracy charge. ($ = 1.479 Swiss Francs)
